Monitoring data is shared with range staff to provide comparisons with unburned reference sites.

Objectives: Objective of this treatment is to establish critical forage and cover for sage-grouse while outcompeting noxious and/or invasive species found in the area.
Planned_Implementation: Approximately 15,000 acres of land burned in the Big Hill Fire would be drill seeded with a mix of native perennial grasses and forbs and an additional 10,000 acres would be drill seeded with a mix of non-native perennial grasses and forbs. Plant species in both mixes were selected based on their ability to establish and persist in the ecological sites common within the burned area. Forb species were specifically selected that are preferred forage by sage-grouse. Determination between using native or non-native mix for a given area was made based on pre-fire plant communities and their overall condition. The native seed mix was selected where the pre-fire vegetation was in reasonably good condition. The non-native mix was selected for areas where cheatgrass occurred in sufficient quantity as to potentially out-compete existing perennial grasses during the recovery period. The non-natives are more vigorous than native species and better able to compete with invasive annual plants.
Actual_Implementation: FY11 funds were used to purchase seed for drill seeding from Regional Seed Warehouse and other numerous vendors at Consolidated Seed Buy, and to pay for cultural clearance contract.\r\nXXXXX completed cultural clearance on 25,000 acres of proposed Big Hill drill seeding area. Standard rangeland drills without depth bands were used, provided by the Vale drill shop.\r\nThe contractor drill seeded 15,000 total acres using 4 tractors, each pulling 3 drill sets. Treatment_Effect_and_Results:
In 2012, the drill row basal gap intercept method was conducted and the percent of basal gaps between perennial grasses less than 100cm averaged 61.9% in non-native mix (Mix 2) plots (6 plots) and 23.7 % in native mix (Mix 1) plots (7 plots); therefore, seeded grasses in non-native seedings were meeting the objective and native seedings were not.

2. Desirable (native and seeded) perennial plant foliar cover in drill seeded areas has not increased 20% and invasive annual grass foliar cover has not decreased 20% compared to control areas; therefore the objective is not being met in any of the allotments or drill mixes (Table 8-4 and Figures 8-1, 8-2, 8-3). Drill seeded plots on average had less or similar desirable foliar cover percentages than control plots, and similar invasive annual grass percent cover in all years (Table 8-4). Site assessment notes indicated that control plots were dominated by Sandberg bluegrass (Poa secunda) and cheatgrass. Cheatgrass (Bromus tectorum) was also either dominant (40-100% cover) or subdominant (10-40% cover) in all drill mix areas, with seeded grasses and Sandberg bluegrass minor (2-10% cover) to subdominant. Drill seeded species, when present were reported in good vigor, as evident in photo of plot GAK1DR11 below.
Overall, average foliar cover of desirable species was less in native mix (Mix 1) than in nonnative/native mix (Mix 2) for all years of monitoring, but was most pronounced in the first year; the native mix averaged 14% while nonnative/native mix averaged 33.5% in 2012, native mix averaged 22.6% while non-native mix averaged 29.2% in 2013, and native mix averaged 25.2% while non-native mix averaged 31% in 2014. Invasive annual grass cover was less at non-native mix sites than native drill sites overall, but only by 3% in 2012, 11% in 2013, and 5% in 2014.
There was a notable difference in foliar cover percentages by allotment in the three years of monitoring. In the Table Butte allotment (Figure 8-3) foliar cover for desirable perennials was very similar at control and drill seeded plots (approximately half of Table Butte was drill seeded with each mix; 5 monitoring plots in native mix, and 4 monitoring plots in non-native mix). While there was an increase in desirable perennials in 2014, the average increase was only 6% in all drill seeded areas and 4% in control areas (Table 8-4). The non-native mix had 6% higher average foliar cover of desirable perennials compared to the native mix; however, the native mix had 10% lower invasive annual grass cover.
In Table Butte pasture 4 both drill mixes were seeded and there was one control plot. The control plot in pasture 4 of Table Butte allotment had significantly less desirable species (mainly Sandberg bluegrass), compared to other control plots and is not typical of control plots. This control plot (CP03) also had the highest cheatgrass foliar cover of the entire fire. Therefore, non-native treatment areas have 30% more desirable foliar cover, and native drill sites have 14% more desirable foliar cover; however there was not a corresponding 20% less annual foliar cover so the objective is not being met. In 2014 cheatgrass foliar cover decreased in the native mix areas (43% in 2013 to 18% in 2014), but maintained constant in the control and non-native mix (32% and 26% foliar cover respectively) (Table 8-5b). Snake River wheatgrass (Elymus wawawaiensis) was the native mix species with the highest foliar cover (4.7%), and Siberian wheatgrass (Agropyron fragile) was the non-native species with highest foliar cover in Table Butte allotment pasture 4 (7.5%). Fourwing salt bush was also found in site assessment observations at non-native drill seeded sites. Bottlebrush squirreltail (Elymus elymoides), Indian ricegrass (Achnatherum hymenoides), and Basin wildrye (Leymus cinereus) were observed in trace amounts. Naturally occurring Sandberg bluegrass was highest in the non-native drill sites (25% foliar cover), while native drill sites had 12%, and the control plot has 3% (Table 8-5b).

In Table Butte pasture 1, areas were drill seeded with the native mix, and there was one control plot. Sandberg bluegrass was the species with the highest cover in all areas of the pasture; in 2014 foliar cover was 28% in the control plot and 23% in the drill seeded plots. This is twice as much Sandberg bluegrass in the native drill seed areas as in pasture 4 (12% foliar cover) (Table 8-5b). Cheatgrass cover was less in pasture 1 than pasture 4; 16% in the control plot and 15% in native drill in pasture 1 compared to 32% and 18% in pasture 4. In all three years of monitoring, cheatgrass cover was static in pasture 1. The native seeded species in pasture 1 with the highest cover was Snake River wheatgrass (4.7%). Siberian wheatgrass from a historic seeding has a similar foliar cover (6.4%).
In the Center allotment, desirable perennial vegetation in the single control plot measurably changed with an increase of 20% from 2012 to 2014, while desirable perennials at drill sites (non-native mix) decreased by 10% (Figure 8-2, Table 8-4). Invasive annual grass cover was similar in 2014 at both control and drill plots in the Center allotment (foliar cover of cheatgrass was 20% in the control plot and 17% in drill plot) (Table 8-5a). Foliar cover of Sandberg bluegrass was higher at control plots than drill plots in Center allotment; 54% in control and 18% in drill (Table 8-5a). Bottlebrush squirreltail naturally recovered in both control and non-native drill sites in Center allotment (foliar cover 7% in control and 4% in drill sites). Additionally, Siberian wheatgrass from a historical seeding was 3% in control sites, and despite being part of the non-native mix in the drill sites was also 3% foliar cover in the drill sites (Table 8-5a). The only non-native drill seeded species observed in Center allotment was Siberian wheatgrass.
In the Blackstone allotment, invasive annual grass foliar cover percent remained higher than desirable perennials, despite an increase in desirable perennials of 15% from 2012-2014 for native drill mix sites (Table 8-4, figure 8-1). Cheatgrass foliar cover was higher than in other allotments overall with 37% foliar cover (Table 8-5a). Bottlebrush squirreltail was the drill seeded species from the native mix with the highest foliar cover in Blackstone allotment (6%). Objectives: The objective is to establish sagebrush, increase forb diversity, and establish early germinating cool season grasses that will reduce the expansion of invasive grasses and weeds on the site as well as prevent erosion to susceptible areas.
Planned_Implementation: A seed mix containing Wyoming big sagebrush, yarrow, and other native forbs would be aerially broadcast seeded across the majority of the area burned in the Big Hill fire during late fall or winter of 2011/2012. Timing of the seed application will ensure seed-to-soil contact prior to winter snow fall or precipitation. These species are paramount to the areas ability to support viable populations of sage-grouse. Seed would be broadcast using an end product contract by either a helicopter or fixed-wing aircraft.
Actual_Implementation:
BLM aerial seeding of 63,100 acres using 2 fixed wing Ag-Thrush aircraft.
Seeding of project began on 1/27/2012 and was completed on 2/3/2012. During project, a few days were short or cancelled due to high winds. Fixed wing aircraft used county road as runway.
Seed (grass/forb/shrub mix) was applied at a rate of 2.7 bulk lbs/acre on 63,100 acres. Fuel break seeding was also done with forage kochia at a rate of 4.6 bulk lbs/acre on 65 acres.
Ground conditions were clear of snow; soil was moist with a few rain events occurring during application.
Treatment_Effect_and_Results:
Objective(s)
1. Attain a density of one sagebrush seedling per 10m\xb2 in suitable areas. Conduct Aerial
Seeding Shrub Hoop monitoring.
2. Quantitative objectives were not tied to aerially seeded forb or grass germination and
survivorship; qualitatively the objective for these groups is to increase forb diversity and
establish sagebrush and cool season (early germinating) perennial grasses. Conduct
Aerial Seeding and Line Point Intercept monitoring and Site Assessments.

2021 Results: 
The objective of one sagebrush (Artemisia tridentata ssp. wyomingensis) seedling per 10m2 has not been met 5 or 10 years post-fire. Seeded sagebrush were uncommon across the burned area in both 2016 and 2021. In 2012, average sagebrush seedling density was less than 0.1 per 10m2, and only trace amounts (<2%) mature sagebrush were seen in 2013 but no seedlings were observed. In 2014 the entire area was surveyed for shrubs with a focus on areas most suitable for sagebrush seedling establishment in the south and east of the fire perimeter. Trace amounts of seedlings were observed in the eastern portion of the fire; none were seed in the southern portion. Sagebrush foliar cover from line point intercept was also trace; 1% in 2012, 0.7% in 2013 and 0.3% in 2014. Small patches of remnant shrubs were observed in the Center allotment in an area that had been both drill and aerially seeded.

Drill and aerially seeded cool season grass cover has not changed substantially between 2014 and 2021 based on qualitative site assessments. Seeded perennial forb species observed in 2012, 2013, 2014 and 2021 included alfalfa, Western yarrow, and Lewis’ flax. Sandberg bluegrass was a subdominant or minor component of the plant community at each plot monitored in 2021 except CP03. Few sagebrush seedlings were observed in suitable sites; therefore, the objective to establish sagebrush is not being met (See photos below).
Aerially seeded locations (including areas also drill seeded) were meeting the objective of cool season perennial grass establishment in 2012, 2013 and 2014. Although aerially seeded grass germination was low, particularly for sand dropseed, Sandberg bluegrass and historically seeded crested/Siberian wheatgrass have recovered. In 2014, site assessments indicated that perennial vegetation was the dominant cover and grasses were in good vigor over the majority of the seeded area; annuals were dominant cover at only three monitoring plots. Overall Sandberg bluegrass was the most abundant cover, other perennial grasses observed in subdominant (10-40%) or dominant composition were bottlebrush squirreltail, Snake River wheatgrass bluebunch wheatgrass. Small patches of existing sagebrush were present throughout. Where annuals were dominant, cheatgrass was the most common annual species and bare soil ranged from a quarter to half of the site.
Perennial forb diversity is also meeting the objective, and although abundance was low across the landscape this was expected because of the low seeding rates Table (8-8). Naturally occurring forbs including hawksbeard (Crepis sp.), phlox (Phlox sp.), globemallow (Sphaeralcea sp.), milkvetch (Astragalus sp.) and wild onion (Allium sp.) larkspur (Delphinium sp.), deathcamas (Zigadenus venosus), buckwheat (Eriogonum sp.), and dusty maiden (Chaenactis douglasii) were present in trace amounts.

The aerial seeding was monitored during the 2007 and 2008 field seasons.

Monitoring in 2008 consisted of 2 transects in chained and seeded areas, and 3 transects in drill-seeded areas and 3 transects in reference areas that were burned but not seeded (see Fig. 1). Each transect was 20 x 300 ft., thereby covering a total area of 6,000 ft. Big sagebrush (Artemisia tridentata) plants were counted within transects. Yarrow, flax and penstemon were not monitored in 2008.
Treatment_Effect_and_Results:
Monitoring conducted in the chained area showed that this area had the highest diversity of perennial grass species.  This area had very little crested wheatgrass present, however there was little present prior to the fire.  Monitoring showed that the aerial seeding objective was achieved at the excellent level. 

The transects that were conducted in the acres of the seeding, found the existing burned vegetation recovering, but found very little of the seeded species. However, it may be just too soon to tell how well this seeding will take. More monitoring will be done in 2008 and provide a better overall picture on results.

There were sage brush, white yarrow, Lewis flax, and Wasatch penstemon seedlings found through out the burn, although it is almost impossible to tell if they are natural or from the aerial seeding. This area will be monitored next year to assess the effectiveness of the aerial seeding.

Sagebrush seeding monitoring was done by reading sagebrush density belt transects at each of the eight previously established transect sites. A three hundred foot baseline tape was stretched at the site, and three transects were read at random points along the baseline. Each belt transect was three hundred feet long and 16 feet wide. One sagebrush plant was found in the burned, drill-seeded site in 2008. No other sagebrush plants were counted in reference, drill- or aerial-seeded sites (Table 1). The dominant and almost exclusive vegetation is crested wheatgrass. Lessons learned:
The practice of chaining dead juniper trees was particularly devastating on soil structure and revegetation. Fig. 2 (below) shows an unchained area allowed to naturally recover. Chained areas (Figs. 3-6), although seeded with native vegetation, show lower levels of both native and exotic revegetation and often present large patches of bare ground (Figs. 3 and 4). In areas with gentle slopes, water runoff combined with disturbances from cattle have caused large gullies through the loose soil (Figs. 5 and 6).

Treatment_Effect_and_Results:
Some seeded species were identified in cover transects, density plots, and site visits by the ESR
monitoring specialists, fire ecologist, and weed treatment specialists. Germination of seeded
grasses occurred during October 2011 following rain events that occurred immediately following
drill seeding. Soil surface disturbance due to drill seeding was low.
Bluebunch wheatgrass, bottlebrush squirreltail, and alfalfa were all observed in drill rows during
site visits in spring and summer 2012 and on May 15, 2013. Western yarrow and sagebrush
seedlings were also observed, although neither species occurred in monitoring transects or
density plots. Grasses recorded as "unidentified" during monitoring were likely seeded plants
that were not yet reproductive. Some plants that were obviously a result of seeding were
flowering in May 2013. On-site native plants that re-sprouted following the fire were also
observed, including bluebunch wheatgrass, bottlebrush squirreltail, Sandberg bluegrass,
Thurber’s needlegrass, penstemon, larkspur, and globemallow. Cheatgrass was common
throughout the burned area and dominant in places. It commonly occurred in drill rows. Cover
data recorded 64% bare ground in 2012 and 27% in 2013.

RECOMMENDATIONS/CONCLUSIONS
Drill and aerial seeding treatments showed good germination and establishment during the first
growing season, despite dry winter and late spring conditions. This area was treated due to
concerns regarding potential dominance of the area by cheatgrass without seeding. Seeding was
done at a low density due to presence of native grasses and forbs expected to recover following
the fire. This, coupled with the use of depth bands, which were required due to the presence of
slick spot peppergrass habitat, may have contributed to the establishment of cheatgrass in drill
rows. Cheatgrass is currently common within the burned area and dominant in portions.
However, the area showed both good establishment of seeded plants and recovery of on-site
natives by the second growing season.

Objectives and Results
1. >50% of seeded species basal gaps are =100cm. Conduct drill row basal gap intercept

In 2017, drill seeded plots had 21.3% greater foliar cover of desirable perennial vegetation than
the untreated plot outside of the exclosure. The average percent foliar cover of exotic annual
vegetation was 15.4% higher in that untreated plot compared to the drill seeded plots. Within the
exclosure, the drill seeded plot had a 21.9% higher average percent foliar cover for desirable
perennial vegetation than the non-drill seeded plot. The non-drill seeded plot also had 38%
higher average foliar cover of exotic annual vegetation (Figure 8-1, 8-2 and Table 8-2).
Since 2015, there was a 40% increase in percent foliar cover of exotic annual vegetation in the
non-drill seeded plot within the exclosure. There was a 6.7% increase in foliar cover of exotic
vegetation in the drill seeded plots. This objective has been met.
Siberian wheatgrass (Agropyron fragile) comprises the majority of the foliar cover at the drill seeded
plots (41%) and the control drill seeded plot (51%). Sandberg bluegrass (Poa secunda)
comprises the majority of the foliar cover at the control plot that was not drill seeded within the
exclosure (50.7%) and the plot in the untreated area outside the exclosure (48%) (Figure 8-1, 8-2
and Table 8-2).

4. Qualitative increase in perennial grass and forb diversity compared to control area.

Objectives:
The area burned by Kern Fire is in need of rehabilitation to minimize soil loss, preserve on-site
productivity, reduce the invasion and increased dominance of undesirable flammable annual plants
and reduce the potential for noxious weed invasion. These objectives can be met by protecting residual
native vegetation communities during a period necessary for recovery of health and vigor and
establishing desirable perennial plant cover in annual vegetation communities. This environmental
assessment analyzes the benefits and risks of implementing rehabilitation actions to establish native
perennial vegetation cover as compared to establishment of desirable non-native perennial species, and
also includes a limited rehabilitation and a no action alternative.
Planned_Implementation:
The proposed action would be to seed approximately 2,160 acres of public land in the burn area using
rangeland drills during the fall of 2000 or spring of 200 1. An estimated 1800 acres of public land
within Oxbow Basin previously dominated by Wyoming big sagebrush and with an understory of
sparse native bunchgrasses would be seeded to a native perennial seed mixture (Seeding Area B,
Figure 2). An additional 360 acres of public land south of Grassy Reservoir and of similar vegetation
type prior to the fire, though more heavily dominated by Medusa-head ryegrass and adjacent to an
existing seeding of created wheatgrass, would be seeded to a non-native perennial seed mixture
(Seeding Area A, Figure 2). Proposed seed mixes are presented in Table 2. The mixes may be altered
slightly depending upon seed availability and lor soil types on site. For instance, compatible forbs or
shrubs such as globemallow (Sphaercea spp.), lupine (Lupinus spp.), four-wing saltbush (Atriplex
canescens), bitterbrush (Purtia tridentata), or scadscale (Atriplex conJertifolia) may be substituted.
Similarly, other varieties of blue bunch wheatgrass or crested wheatgrass may be substituted as
available. All seed when mixed would be treated with organic seed coating to enhance germination
success and seedling survival. The remaining 9,908 acres of public and private land within the fire
boundary would not be seeded due to steepness of slopes or its location within islands which did not
burn (Figure 2).

1. Density of aerially seeded forbs in suitable areas is an average of greater than or equal to
0.5 plants per 10 m2.

2. Conduct a qualitative assessment of the seeded species phenology.
Actual_Implementation: A total of 5,974 acres were aerially seeded near active greater sage-grouse leks in 2017 in Coal\r\nMine Basin, Shares Basin, and Rockville Pasture 7 lek area ranging in elevation from 4,000 to\r\n5,200 ft. These areas were seeded at 100% coverage (Appendix A: Table A-25).
Treatment_Effect_and_Results:
In 2019 and 2020 the areas seeded with the sage-grouse preferred forb mix were surveyed for all plant species using meandering transects within each seeded polygon for Rockville Pasture 7, Shares Basin Pasture 1, Blackstock Springs 1 and Succor Creek Pasture 1. While native forb richness and abundance were moderate to high in these areas, (11 native forb species in Shares Basin 1 to 27 in Rockville 7) the only species found that were in the sage-grouse preferred seed mix were Balsamorhiza sagittata, Astragalus filipies, and Crepis occidentalis, which may or may not have originated from the seeding.

In 2017, the areas seeded with sage-grouse preferred forb mix were surveyed for all plant species
using meandering transects within each seeded polygon. Plant species were recorded throughout
each transect while targeting the seeded sage-grouse preferred forbs. All seeded species were
located in at least one of the four seeding areas. Penstemon eatonii was found in the highest
quantities but never approached the objective of 0.5 plants per 10 m2 in suitable areas. Most
Lomatium dissectum, Crepis occidentalis, Balsamorhiza sagittata and Astragalus filipies
individuals that were observed were established plants that were likely not the result of the aerial
seeding, although a few A. filipies seedlings were found in the aerially seeded portion of the
Succor Creek allotment. Penstemon accuminatus and Dalea ornata were found within the
seeded portion of Shares Basin in Shares Basin Pasture 1 and Hardtrigger Pasture 4.
The aerially seeded portion of Sands Basin Pasture 4 had the highest number and quantity of
sage-grouse preferred forbs and is closest to meeting the objective. This is likely because this
area had the most suitable areas for seed germination, i.e. areas where shrubs were present before
the Soda fire and therefore burned hot leaving bare soil. This area also is in a Loamy 11-13
ecological site and therefore has consistently deeper soils than the other areas that were seeded
with this mix. Six of the ten seeded species were found in this area; A. filipies, B. sagittata, C.
occidentalis, Malacothrix glabrata, P. eatonii, and Sphaeralcea spp. Where seeded species were
found they exceeded the objective but seeded forbs were not found in all suitable areas.
In 2016, it is likely that the individual forbs detected during monitoring were plants that existed
prior to the Soda fire and not as a result of the seeding. Crepis was detected in 13 pastures and
B. sagittata was detected in 12 of the 14 pastures monitored. A. filipies was detected in half of
the 14 pastures. Penstemon, Malacothrix, and Sphaeralcea were not detected in any of the
pastures. The Jackson Creek allotment had the highest density of B. sagittata and second highest
of Crepis; all pastures monitored in this allotment were treated with aerial herbicide during the
spring of 2016 (see Part 6, S5 for details).

2. Plant phenology was not assessed in 2016. In 2017 the majority of the emerged seeded perennial
forbs were either flowering or fruiting at the time of monitoring.

Objectives:
Objective: The objective of the seeding treatment is to establish perennial-dominated plant communities within 3 years. The
following grass, forb, and shrub density objectives are based on ecological site potential.
The drill seed treatments would be considered successful if:
The seeded grass and forb species reach densities of:
? 3 plants per square meter for grasses
? 0.25 plants per square meter for forbs
Planned_Implementation: Drill Seed Mix #1 would be used in areas that were occupied by sagebrush-steppe communities in good ecological condition prior to the fire. This seed mix was designed to address the potential for cheatgrass expansion, provide cover and food for sage-grouse and other sagebrush-steppe obligate wildlife, and provide structural and compositional diversity to decrease fine fuel continuity.
Actual_Implementation:
Three seed mixes were used in four drill seeding areas:
Bruneau River Drill Seeding – The project consisted of drill
seeding 5,289 acres within the Kinyon Road Fire near the Bruneau
River with two different seed mixes, Mix 1 and the Bruneau
Scenic Overlook mix (listed below, see Map 1). Two rangeland
drills and three contractor-furnished Oliver drills were used and all
discs had depth bands. Seed was applied in dry to moist conditions.
The contractor for the project was Jarolimek Farm and Rangeland
Drill Seeding of Twin Falls, Idaho. The seed was pre-mixed by
ESR staff. The project was started on October 7, 2012, and
completed on November 13, 2012.

Devil Creek Drill Seeding – This project consisted of drill seeding
6,395 acres within the Kinyon Road Fire near Devil Creek with
Seed Mix One (listed below, see Map 2). Four rangeland drills were
used and all discs had depth bands. Seed was applied in dry to
moist conditions. The last block by Tuana Butte was completed in
very wet to muddy conditions. The contractor for this area was Loy
Pehrson of Buhl, Idaho. The seed was pre-mixed by ESR staff. The
project was started on October 9, 2012, and completed on
November 26, 2012.

Coonskin Drill Seeding – This project consisted of drill seeding
6,285 acres within the Kinyon Road Fire in the Coonskin Butte /
Kinyon Road area with two seed mixes, Mix 1 and Mix 2 (listed
below, see Map 2). Six rangeland drills were used and all discs had
depth bands. Seed was applied in dry to moist conditions most of
the time; the last of the seeding was done in wet to muddy
conditions. The ground was frozen early in the morning on the last
two days. The seed was pre-mixed by ESR staff. The contractor for
the project was Absaroka Construction, Inc., of Buhl, Idaho. The
projects was started on October 5, 2012, and completed on December 3, 2012.

Juniper Draw Drill Seeding – The project consisted of drill seeding
3,813 acres within the Kinyon Road Fire in the Coonskin Butte /
Kinyon Road area with two seed mixes, Mix 1 and Mix 2 (listed
below, see Map 2). Up to 14 rangeland drills were used and all but
two of the drills did not have discs with depth bands. The project
was completed by ESR and Fire staff. These areas had been
contracted, but due to issues with the contractor, these acres were
removed from the contract. Seed was applied in very wet to muddy
conditions. There were early mornings when the ground was
frozen; conditions improved later in the morning. The seed was premixed
by ESR staff. The project was started on November 28,
2012, and completed on December 8, 2012.
Treatment_Effect_and_Results:
Drill Mix 1
For the first two years, areas seeded with Drill Mix 1 had spotty establishment, but seeded
grasses and forbs were observed in drill rows in most locations. In some cases, seedlings were
visually difficult to detect because they were obscured by annual vegetation such as Russian
thistle and tumble mustard. In addition, plant establishment was staggered. In 2014, both large
reproductive and smaller non-reproductive plants were present and in 2015 further growth and
additional recruitment were observed. Inconsistent establishment was likely due to the use of
depth bands, which did not result in uniform seed burial. Establishment of seeded forbs is not
well reflected in the monitoring data. However, all three species were observed to occur in most
seeded areas. Sagebrush seedlings occurred as scattered patches or individuals during 2014 and
2015 field visits.
Recovery of on-site natives was observed, including Sandberg bluegrass, bottlebrush squirreltail,
western wheatgrass, and Thurber's needlegrass. Some of the sagebrush communities that burned
in the fire were old crested wheatgrass seedings that had been reinvaded by sagebrush. In these
cases, crested wheatgrass occurred in the understory at low densities and it was unknown
whether cover would be adequate post-fire to stabilize the burned sites. In cases where crested
wheatgrass did not recover at high density, seeded species established and diversified these old
crested wheatgrass seedings.

FY 17
Monitoring plots were revisited for the 5th year monitoring by Chicago Botanical interns in the summer of 2017. Qualitative assessments were completed and included a general plot description, species inventory, and photo documentation. For the 5th year monitoring year, seven plots were revisited for qualitative assessments. Plots visited include 001, 002, 004, 006, 009, 010, and 012.
The Kinyon Road rehabilitation can be addressed geographically, as the treatments were divided separately into the eastern and western burned areas. The focus of this summary will be on the west side, also known as the Bruneau Overlook area, as heavy noxious weed infestations and unsuccessful drill seedings here were concerning. Due to the good establishment of the drill seed treatments on the eastern side, attention and resources should be focused on the Bruneau Overlook area in future treatments.
On the eastern side of Kinyon, drill seedings were highly successful. Perennial grasses, particularly bluebunch wheatgrass and Siberian wheatgrass, dominate the landscape, and the bare ground among them supports a high diversity of forbs with relatively low cheatgrass establishment. Though sagebrush seedlings were either not found or found in extremely low amounts in these areas, many sagebrush islands were seen near monitoring points, and could potentially re-seed the area regardless of the success of shrub seedings. Invasive weeds such as rush skeletonweed, halogeton, and Russian thistle are present, but are not an imminent threat, especially considering the health and expanse of the perennial grasses. It would be valuable for future projects to assess why the eastern Kinyon plantings were so successful compared to the Bruneau Overlook area.
The Bruneau Overlook seeding treatments have been moderately successful but present several challenges. In some areas, drill-seeded perennial bunchgrass populations are vigorous and extensive with good forb diversity, but cheatgrass density is still high. Most areas on this side of the Kinyon fire are cheatgrass-Sandberg’s bluegrass dominated sites with low forb diversity, and drill-seeded perennials are not competing as well. Few to no sagebrush seedlings were seen across the area, and sagebrush islands were also rarer. Noxious and invasive weed populations also present a problem.
A main concern for this area is extremely dense invasive weed populations, particularly Russian thistle. The Bruneau Overlook area is being overtaken by this dominant weed, and full hillsides of robust Russian thistle were found near monitoring points (Photo 1). The eastern monitoring area also showed some large Russian thistle populations. Russian thistle is likely to continue dominating the Kinyon Road area unless significant control measures are taken. Rush skeletonweed is also present across the Kinyon Road fire area, though to a much lesser extent than the thistle. It has the potential to continue spreading and impeding the advancement of perennial bunchgrasses. Chemical treatments in the Bruneau Overlook area on Russian thistle and rush skeletonweed would be most efficient in stopping the spread of these two species, though mechanical treatments on extremely dense Russian thistle patches could also be valuable.
Kinyon Road Fire (G1CH) FY2022 Monitoring – 10th Year 33
Precipitation data is from the Twin Buttes and Horse Butte RAWS stations, which are northeast of the burned area and southwest of the burned area, respectively. Monitoring reports at the first, second- and third-year mark illuminate a trend towards higher precipitation following treatment years, along with later summer and fall rains. This factor may have contributed to higher weed establishment and lower drill seed success. Previous reports also mention soil movement that filled in drill rows and lessened the establishment rate at Bruneau Overlook sites. Compounding this was the inefficient depth band use on the shrub seedings, consequently the first three years of monitoring found no shrub establishment in the monitoring sites. Upon qualitative monitoring at the five-year mark, scattered immature Wyoming big sagebrush were found in only half of the monitoring sites for all of Kinyon. Multiple factors led to both the low shrub establishment throughout Kinyon and the partial success of drill seed treatments in Bruneau Overlook.

Plots visited include 002, 003, 004, 005, 007, 008, 009, 010, 011, 013, 015, 019 021, and 023. Data collected included a general plot description, species inventory, and photo documentation.

• Most desired herbaceous perennial plants are producing seed.

Treatment_Effect_and_Results:
Bruneau Overlook Mix
The Bruneau Overlook Mix was used in areas near the edge of the Bruneau River canyon with
the driest site conditions. Seeding establishment was spotty with some areas showing little or no
germination of seeded species. Other areas had good establishment of primarily Indian ricegrass.
Recovery of on-site natives was low due to extremely dry conditions and possible wind scouring.
In some areas near the Bruneau Canyon rim it appeared that some soil movement had occurred,
filling in drill rows. No sagebrush seedlings were observed. About 200 acres of the area was redrilled
without depth bands in September 2013 using Fuels program funding. About 400 acres
was planned; re-treatment was curtailed by the federal government furlough, then by weather.
Germination and establishment of plants resulting from retreatment were observed in some areas
in June 2014. Good establishment of seeded plants in the retreatment areas was observed in June
2015.

FY 17
Monitoring plots were revisited for the 5th year monitoring by Chicago Botanical interns in the summer of 2017. Qualitative assessments were completed and included a general plot description, species inventory, and photo documentation. For the 5th year monitoring year, seven plots were revisited for qualitative assessments. Plots visited include 001, 002, 004, 006, 009, 010, and 012.
The Kinyon Road rehabilitation can be addressed geographically, as the treatments were divided separately into the eastern and western burned areas. The focus of this summary will be on the west side, also known as the Bruneau Overlook area, as heavy noxious weed infestations and unsuccessful drill seedings here were concerning. Due to the good establishment of the drill seed treatments on the eastern side, attention and resources should be focused on the Bruneau Overlook area in future treatments.
On the eastern side of Kinyon, drill seedings were highly successful. Perennial grasses, particularly bluebunch wheatgrass and Siberian wheatgrass, dominate the landscape, and the bare ground among them supports a high diversity of forbs with relatively low cheatgrass establishment. Though sagebrush seedlings were either not found or found in extremely low amounts in these areas, many sagebrush islands were seen near monitoring points, and could potentially re-seed the area regardless of the success of shrub seedings. Invasive weeds such as rush skeletonweed, halogeton, and Russian thistle are present, but are not an imminent threat, especially considering the health and expanse of the perennial grasses. It would be valuable for future projects to assess why the eastern Kinyon plantings were so successful compared to the Bruneau Overlook area.
The Bruneau Overlook seeding treatments have been moderately successful but present several challenges. In some areas, drill-seeded perennial bunchgrass populations are vigorous and extensive with good forb diversity, but cheatgrass density is still high. Most areas on this side of the Kinyon fire are cheatgrass-Sandberg’s bluegrass dominated sites with low forb diversity, and drill-seeded perennials are not competing as well. Few to no sagebrush seedlings were seen across the area, and sagebrush islands were also rarer. Noxious and invasive weed populations also present a problem.
A main concern for this area is extremely dense invasive weed populations, particularly Russian thistle. The Bruneau Overlook area is being overtaken by this dominant weed, and full hillsides of robust Russian thistle were found near monitoring points (Photo 1). The eastern monitoring area also showed some large Russian thistle populations. Russian thistle is likely to continue dominating the Kinyon Road area unless significant control measures are taken. Rush skeletonweed is also present across the Kinyon Road fire area, though to a much lesser extent than the thistle. It has the potential to continue spreading and impeding the advancement of perennial bunchgrasses. Chemical treatments in the Bruneau Overlook area on Russian thistle and rush skeletonweed would be most efficient in stopping the spread of these two species, though mechanical treatments on extremely dense Russian thistle patches could also be valuable.

Compounding this was the inefficient depth band use on the shrub seedings, consequently the first three years of monitoring found no shrub establishment in the monitoring sites. Upon qualitative monitoring at the five-year mark, scattered immature Wyoming big sagebrush were found in only half of the monitoring sites for all of Kinyon. Multiple factors led to both the low shrub establishment throughout Kinyon and the partial success of drill seed treatments in Bruneau Overlook.

Objectives: To establish native perennial vegetation within the burn perimeter to maintain sage-grouse habitat and\r\nlimit the amount of non-native invasive species cover post burn.
Planned_Implementation:
Aerial and drill seeding: Seed native grasses and forbs in areas appropriate for these species.

Using existing vegetation maps, Ecological Site Descriptions (ESDs), aerial imagery and a
Burned Area Reflectance Classification (BARC) map, proposed seeding polygons were
delineated. This information was also used to determine appropriate seed mixes. Seeded species
are based on site potential, while considering seed availability and cost. In addition, specific
cultivars of the species chosen were selected based on seedling vigor and ability to germinate
and persist on low precipitation sites. Consideration was also given to vegetation structural
diversity of the site, habitat values, and ability to compete against invasive species. The AFO
BLM staff identified the areas within the burn where habitat values for sage-grouse were highly
impacted and special emphasis was placed on restoring native vegetation to these areas. High
priority areas were primarily higher elevation nesting and summer habitat. In addition, the AFO
staff also worked with the Natural Resource Conservation Service (NRCS) in Reno and
Professor Stringham form the University of Nevada-Reno (UNR) to develop seed mixes that
would be appropriate based on site conditions. Hand planting and aerial seeding sites were also
delineated using the same methodology.
Actual_Implementation:
FY2014: total of 800 acres were surveyed for archeological concerns
between September 1 and September 30 by Applegate Field Office
(AFO) cultural staff. Areas of concern were staked and marked with
flagging to identify the boundary of the cultural sites.

FY2015: A total of 458 acres were seeded out of the 800 acres that were
originally designated for drill seeding. Due to archeological
concerns, approximately 130 acres were eliminated from drill
seeding and were designated for aerial seeding instead. Seed was
purchased from the Boise Regional Seed Warehouse in September
of 2014. Seed arrived in late October of 2014. Drill seeding was
accomplished using a combination of range drill rented from Vale,
Oregon and agency dozers from Hollister, California and
Susanville, California. Drill seeding operations took approximately
two weeks to complete.
Treatment_Effect_and_Results:
FY15:
Quantitative monitoring using quadrates was completed during the 2015 field season. Both
seeded grass species and forbs were counted using a one meter by one meter quad. Data was
collected every 2.5 meters along a 25 meter transect. Transects were arranged in a spoke pattern
using 3 transects. Transects were oriented at 0 degrees, 120 degrees and 240 degrees. Based on
the monitoring results, some of the seeding polygons that were sampled meet the objectives
outlined in the Coleman Fire ES&R plan. Based on monitoring data collected during the 2015
field season, approximately 54.31% of surveyed acres had met the established criteria, 26.67% of
surveyed acres had partially met the established criteria, and 19.01% have yet to be surveyed to
determine if the established criteria had been met. These percentages are based on drill seeded
acres surveyed during the 2015 field season (see map 2 for more details).

Objectives: For the purposes of biotic integrity, establish densities of native forbs to 1 per\r\nsquare meter, native shrubs to 0.3 per square meter, grasses 3 per square meter within 2-5\r\nyears.
Planned_Implementation:
Drill Seeding
A total of approximately 1,064 acres of BLM administered lands would be drill seeded in the fall/winter of 2017/2018 (FY18) with species appropriate for the site based on resistance, resilience, and ecological site descriptions. Drill seeding would take place in areas of gentle topography conducive to drill seeding. Treatment areas are detailed below.

High Elevation Mix -Drill seed approximately 413 acres of PHMA Greater sage-grouse habitat, crucial summer elk and summer range pronghorn habitat with a mixture of bluebunch wheatgrass, Sherman big bluegrass, Great Basin wildrye, Indian ricegrass, Utah sweetvetch, sainfoin, and antelope bitterbrush.
Actual_Implementation:
The High Elevation Drill Treatment seed mix was applied via rangeland drill to the
public burned land in accordance with the ecological sites and elevation and was comprised of
Indian Ricegrass, Bluebunch Wheatgrass, Big Sandberg’s Bluegrass, Antelope Bitterbrush, Utah
Sweetvetch, Sainfoin, and Basin Wildrye.

Confirmed by Monitoring and RIPS Reports.
Treatment_Effect_and_Results:
Density: The High Elevation Drill Treatment seed mix was applied via rangeland drill to the
public burned land in accordance with the ecological sites and elevation and was comprised of
Indian Ricegrass, Bluebunch Wheatgrass, Big Sandberg’s Bluegrass, Antelope Bitterbrush, Utah
Sweetvetch, Sainfoin, and Basin Wildrye. Rehabilitation objectives of the treatment are
considered successfully met when one native forb per square meter, 0.3 native shrubs per square
meter, and three grasses per square meter are established.
2018: In the AIM plots that fell within this seeding treatment (Plot 01) the rehabilitation
objectives in the first growing season have not been met, though there is evidence of progress
towards success. There were 0.17 seeded grasses per square meter in 2018 monitoring and 0.17
seeded forbs per square meter. Seeded shrub seedlings were not found in the treatment area. The
lack of winter precipitation in the 2017-2018 winter may have also contributed to the inability of
the antelope bitterbrush to establish and persist on the sites. The dry conditions may have also
contributed to the low density of seeded forbs and shrubs.
2019: There were 5.75 seeded grasses per square meter in 2019 monitoring and no seeded shrubs
or forbs observed in the density frames. There was a reduction in recovery of grasses on the site
as well. These observations are counter to what would be expected with normal temperatures and
increased precipitation. Regrowth of thickspike wheatgrass (Elymus lanceolatus) and Sandberg
bluegrass (Poa secunda), small-form grasses, and bluebunch wheatgrass (Pseudoroegneria
spicata) was evident on the site.
2020: Seeded grasses were measured in abundance, and some seeded forbs were recorded but no seeded shrubs were observed. Recovery of small and large-form grasses was evident.
2022: Seeded grasses increased from 2020 but seeded forbs dropped back to not being observed along with seeded shrubs. Native regrowth however shows strong signs of reestablishment with 22.6/m2 large and small form grasses combined, 12.6/m2 forbs, and 2.9/m2. While it is ideal to see seeded species in the density plots high levels of native regrowth is promising for rehabilitation of the overall site.

AIM Data Results 
Cover 
2018: Average foliar canopy cover was 60.7% in the treatment area in 2018. Bare ground was still at 24%, which indicates the area needs more time to recover. The foliar cover was comprised of 26.7% cover of a mix of rhizomatous and deep-rooted perennial grasses including western and bluebunch wheatgrass. Annual forb foliar cover was a mix of natives and annuals. Cheatgrass had a low foliar cover of 14%, while perennial forbs were robustly competing with 9.4%. Recovering shrubs had 8.1% cover. Seeded species were not greatly contributing to cover as the native post-fire regrowth of desirable perennials was heeding their gains. 
2019: Average canopy foliar cover was higher in 2019 observations – an increase of 24%. All functional groups showed an increase in cover, possibly explained by extra precipitation. Perennial grasses had the largest jump in canopy cover along with perennial and annual forbs. Sandberg’s bluegrass (Poa secunda), cheatgrass (Bromus tectorum), and thickspike wheatgrass (Elymus lanceolatus) had the highest cover on the site (24.0%, 23.3%, and 16.0% respectively). 
2020: Average canopy foliar cover was moderately high at 58%. Cover was dominated by perennial species including bluebunch wheatgrass, mountain snowberry, and thickspike wheatgrass. Unfortunately, desert madwort and cheatgrass had cover at 8.0% and 7.3%, respectively. 
2022: Average foliar cover was high at 76.0% - an increase of 18% from 2020’s observations. Perennial grass cover dominated at 24.7%, followed by annual forbs at 10.7%. Perennial grass cover did however decrease by nearly 6% from 2020 and shrubs also had a reduction from 22.0% in 2020 down to 7.0% in 2022. Perennial species did still have more foliar coverage on the plot than annual species overall.
Gaps and Erosion 
2018: Gaps in canopy cover that were the size and frequency observed in the drill seeding treatment (the majority were greater than 50 cm) have allowed wind and water erosion to occur on the plots, degrading the hydrologic function and soil and site stability. Over half of the average 25 meter transects are gaps in cover greater than 25 centimeters. Wind and water erosion were minimally affecting the soil and site stability on the plot in 2018: there were only very short and rare water flow patterns and few pedestals observed. However, the presence of a gully and increased deposition/runoff along with few pedestals and water flow patterns indicated an increase in erosion at the site. 
2019: Gaps in canopy cover were typically from 51 to 100 cm long. Gaps represented 5.1% of the average 25m transects, leaving 23.7% of those transects under canopy cover. 
2020: Gaps were primarily between 51 and 100 cam long. All gaps represented 39.5% of the average 25m transects. The same gully was observed, along with some pedestalling and water flow patterns and common deposition/runoff. This indicates some fluctuation in erosion on the site. 
2022: Gaps in the two smaller size range remained fairly similar to their observations in 2020. However, the two larger size ranges had decreases from 9.6% to 0.0% in the 101-200cm range and 6.4% to 2.8% in the >200cm range from 2020 to 2022. The decrease in gap sizes along with no observations of soil erosion on plot show good signs of overall plot rehabilitation.

Seeded grasses exceeded density objectives, as there were 5.17 seeded grasses per square meter

needs to be rested until the plants achieve more robust basal and canopy growth. Neither seeded
forbs nor shrubs were not found in first year monitoring. The lack of winter precipitation in the
2017-2018 winter may have contributed to the inability of the shrubs and forbs to establish and
persist on the site.
2019: In the second growing season, the same amount of seeded grasses were observed and a slight increase in seeded forbs was observed. Furthermore, recovery of native grasses like Sandberg bluegrass (Poa secunda), a small-form perennial grass, and squirreltail (Elymus elymoides) and needle and thread grass (Hesperostipa comata), large-form bunch grasses, was less than that observed in 2018. These observations are not what would be expected given the increased precipitation although seeded species are still showing signs of establishing on the sites.
2020: Seeded grasses were again observed in abundance. No seeded forb observations were made but seeded sagebrush was identified in Plot 02.
2022: Rehabilitation objectives have not been met for this plot with no seeded shrubs or forbs observed. Additionally, seeded grasses decreased from 10.0/m2 in 2020 to 2.2/m2 and native regrowth of forbs and shrubs were not observed at all. This plot is showing signs of decreased progress towards meeting rehabilitation goals. 

2018 Cover: The presence of bare ground was double that of foliar cover in the first growing season,
which indicates the area needs more time to recover. The foliar cover was comprised of 3.7%
seeded Siberian wheatgrass cover, which was competing with a multitude of annual, invasive
plants, including cheatgrass (4.3%) and the 3.7% annual wheatgrass (Eremopyron triticeum)
cover. Halogeton or “salt-lover” (8% cover) was a prominent forb in the treatment area,
especially on AIM Plot 06, which was located in a disturbed Sodic Terrace along an ephemeral
drainage. The halogeton, which changes the soil chemistry by bringing salt to the top layer of the
soil, is of particular concern, especially if perennial seeded species are unable to compete with
the invasive succulent.
2019 Cover: Annual grasses composed the highest proportion of functional groups cover (42.3%). Second to that was perennial grasses at 23.5%. Seeded Siberian wheatgrass increased from 2018 observations to 16.0%. However, cheatgrass and annual wheatgrass have increased to 24.3% (the highest cover of a plant on the sites) and 18.0% respectively. Halogeton was primarily focused in AIM Plot 06 and displayed a slight increase from 2018 observations to 8.3% cover. The plant is still a concern for the seeding on that site.
2020 Cover: Average canopy foliar cover overall was moderately low. Cover was dominated by annual cheatgrass (19.7%) and annual wheatgrass (10.3%). Most abundant perennial species were Siberian wheatgrass (8.3%), Indian ricegrass (0.7%), and Thurber’s needlegrass (0.3%). Collectively, annual species had higher cover on the plots than did perennial species.
2022: Average foliar cover was again, moderately low at 22.0% total. Only perennial and annual grasses were observed with cheatgrass dominating at 15.6% compared to perennials at 0.5%.

centimeters long, the largest measured threshold category. Canopy gaps of this size and
frequency have allowed wind and water erosion to occur on the plots, degrading the hydrologic
function and soil and site stability. Over 90% of the surface area consists of gaps greater than 25
centimeters.

2020: Monitoring results indicate that the seeded species are trying to establish at these sites. Grasses have met rehabilitation objectives while forbs and shrubs have not, although the forbs are trying to come in on the sites. There was an allotment closure issued for the Gamble Individual allotment in the East Delano Mountain pasture. The allotment closure objective of three perennial species has been met but it is advised that the area receives appropriate grazing management so seeded forb and shrub species may establish, especially the black sagebrush and gooseberryleaf globemallow and Utah sweetvetch, which would add biotic diversity and sage grouse preferred forbs and shrub cover to the sites. 
2022: Monitoring results indicate that the site is experiencing soil instability, site erosion, and an overall decrease in plot health. The combination of low stability, high disturbance, and the abundance of cheatgrass on the plot would suggest that some further intervention (e.g. more seeding, herbicide, etc.) could be needed to keep the plot from becoming a disturbed cheatgrass monoculture. Density Results

2020: Foliar cover reduced dramatically from years before, with the largest reduction being observed in perennial and annual grasses with smaller reductions throughout each of the indicators. 
2022: Foliar cover was moderately high at 77.3%, an increase of 25.4% from 2020. Perennial grasses increased to 43.2% from 34.7% in 2020. In conjunction with the decrease of cheatgrass by 0.6% and annual forbs by 9.6%, the increase in perennial grasses, perennial forbs, and shrubs, the health of this plot appears to have improved since 2020.
Gaps and Erosion 
2018: Gaps in canopy cover were infrequent and short. Canopy gaps of the size and frequency measured on the plots have not allowed wind and water erosion to occur. Wind and water erosion were minimally affecting the soil and site stability on the plot: there few pedestals were present in 2018. 
2019: Canopy gaps were mostly between 25 and 50 cm long. This is similar to 2018 observations. A reduction in pedestalling and water flow patterns was observed, indicating more stability on the site.

Since the regrowth of native, perennial forbs was so low, the area would benefit from the forb-seeding establishment, as well as the seeded sagebrush. 
2019: Monitoring results in the treatment area have shown that rehabilitation objectives have not been met in the second growing season. No seeded forbs were observed and a reduced amount of seeded shrubs were observed. This is unexpected given more normal temperatures and increased precipitation in the area. The native recovery for grasses on the site is noteworthy. There was and allotment closure issued for the Gamble Individual allotment in the East Delano Mountain pasture. It is advised that the area receives additional rest as it would benefit from the forb-seeding establishment, as well as the seeded sagebrush.

Seed would be applied using an every other swath pattern (2,104 actual seeded acres). Aerial seeding would be coordinated with snowfall conditions, if time permits. Aerial seed mixtures are described in detail below.

Aerial Mix B -Approximately 1,371 acres of PHMA and OHMA Greater sage-grouse habitat, crucial summer and crucial winter elk, mule deer winter, and pronghorn summer range habitat, would be aerially seeded with black sagebrush, Wyoming big sagebrush, bluebunch wheatgrass, Indian ricegrass, Sandberg's bluegrass, and blue flax using an every other swath pattern (686 actual acres seeded).
Actual_Implementation:
The Aerial Mix B Treatment seed mix was applied via fix-wing aircraft to the public
burned land in accordance with the ecological sites and elevation and was comprised of Black
Sagebrush, Wyoming Big Sagebrush, Blue Flax, Indian Ricegrass, Sandberg’s Bluegrass, and
Bluebunch Wheatgrass.
Treatment_Effect_and_Results:
Aerial Mix B Treatment Results
Density Results: 
Rehabilitation objectives will be considered met when one seeded forb, 0.3 seeded shrubs, and three seeded grasses per square meter are observed. 
2018: The rehabilitation objectives in the first growing season have not been met. The seeded species are showing unimpressive progress towards success, especially the seeded shrubs, which were not found to be establishing in the first growing season on any of the three plots. The aerially seeded grasses and forbs had the biggest successes in AIM Plot 08, which is a higher elevation pinyon pine and juniper site. Forbs have had a small amount of success by establishing at a density of 0.2 plants per square meter and seeded grasses have established at a density of 0.58 plants per square meter. 
2019: In 2019 monitoring results, a higher amount of seeded grasses were observed. This primarily was due to observations of Sandberg’s bluegrass which could also be considered part of native recovery on the site. Some seeded Wyoming big sagebrush was observed with an increase in large-form and decrease in small-form species as well. The small amount of seeded species establishment and native recovery is somewhat unexpected for the site given the improvement in weather over the past year. 
2020: No seeded shrubs were observed. Some seeded forbs were observed and seeded grasses were observed in abundance. Recovery of large and small-form perennial grasses was also observed. 
2022: Rehabilitation objectives for this plot have not been fully met. Shrubs and grasses meet the criteria with 0.7/m2 and 18.9/m2 observed but forbs fell short at 0.1. However, native regrowth of shrubs shows signs of establishment at 2.8/m2 along with shrubs at 0.8/m2. 
AIM Data Results: 
Cover 
2018: The bare ground was more prevalent than foliar cover by 34.7% in the first growing season, which indicates that more time is necessary for rest and growth. The foliar cover was comprised of 15.3% native, perennial grass cover. Tree cover represented 10.0% foliar cover. Perennial forbs and shrubs will benefit from higher precipitation in the second growing season as they were not observed this season. 
2019: Foliar cover was dominated by perennial grasses (44.7%), primarily due to Sandberg’s bluegrass (14.9%) and Siberian wheatgrass (8.2%) observations, similar to 2018 results. Second to this was the annual forb observations (24.7%) with desert madwort and prickly lettuce making up 8.4% and 5.8% of foliar cover. Halogeton, an invasive species, was observed on the plots and made up 5.1% foliar cover. Tree cover was reduced from 2018 observations to 3.3% cover. 
2020: Cover was moderately low. Cover was dominated by perennial Siberian wheatgrass and Sandberg bluegrass and annual wheatgrass. Cheatgrass was observed on the site with low cover (4.7%) along with desert madwort (2.2%). Collectively, perennial species dominated cover over annual species on the sites. 
2022: Cover was moderate at 60.0%, dominated by perennial grasses (19.8%), followed by annual forbs (8.3), and annual grass reducing from 4.7% in 2020 to 3.2% in 2022. Most indicators saw a reduction in cover with perennial grasses taking the biggest hit, losing around 15% of its cover.

Gaps and Erosion 
2018: Gaps in canopy cover were long and frequently occurring, allowing wind and water erosion to occur. The hydrologic function and soil and site stability have been impacted due to these gaps and the lack of perennial canopy cover on the sites. Very short and rare water flow patterns, common pedestals, few and short rills, and rare soil deposition/runoff gave proof of the impaired soil and site stability in 2018. 
2019: Gaps remained very similar to results from the 2018 season. Although canopy cover has increased significantly, gaps are still common enough to make the site susceptible to wind and water erosion. In 2019 observations, there were decreased observations of rills, similar observations of common pedestalling and water flow patterns, and increased observations of common deposition/runoff. This indicates soil instability on the site. 
2020: Gaps decreased across all ranges and were primarily between 51 and 100 cm long. Fewer pedestals were observed along with no deposition/runoff and no water flow patterns. This indicates increased stability on the site. 
2022: Gaps increased in each size range; the bottom 3 size classes saw the largest increases with >200cm only seeing an increase of 2.2% from 0.6% last year. The reduction of foliar cover across the plot likely had an impact on gap increasing across the plot but a lack of soil instability and plot degradation across the plot means the gap increase may not be a bad sign of rehabilitation.
Species Richness
2022: Species richness increased from 2019 from 31 individual species observed to 36. Perennial forbs and shrubs increased while annual forbs reduced by 2. Perennial grasses remained the same and perennials overall continued to outnumber the annuals observed.
Recommendations 
2018: The seeded forbs, grasses, and shrubs have not successfully established and the area needs to remain closed for another growing season or two. If the upcoming winter and second year growing season receive normal to above normal precipitation and snowpack is maintained by cooler winter temperatures, the seeded species have a higher chance at establishing and meeting rehabilitation objectives. Since the regrowth of native, perennial forbs was so low, the area would benefit from the seeded forb establishment, as well as the seeded sagebrush. 
2019: The seeded forbs, grasses, and shrubs have not successfully established. An allotment closure has been issued for the Gamble Individual allotment in the East Delano Mountain pasture. The allotment closure objective of three perennial species per square meter has been met but it is advised that the area receives additional rest. The improved weather conditions did not appear to help the seeded species establishment. Since the regrowth of native, perennial forbs was so low, the area would benefit from the seeded forb establishment, as well as the seeded sagebrush, to provide various wildlife forage. 
2020: Seeded grasses have successfully established on the plot. However, seeded forbs and shrubs still need more time to come in. An allotment closure has been issued for the Gamble Individual allotment in the East Delano Mountain. The allotment closure objective of three perennial species per square meter has been met but it is advised that the area receives proper grazing management so that seeded species may have more of a chance to grow back in. 
2022: Seeded grasses continue to show signs of establishment on the plot and seeded shrubs and forbs show signs of beginning to establish on the plot. The overall health of this site appears positive but continued appropriate grazing management is recommended to allow forbs and shrubs more time to fully establish roots if possible.
