2022 ESR Monitoring Results
S2 Drill Seeding/S3 Aerial Mid-Elevation 
Dry Gulch AIM Plot 01A is located in a Rangeland Loamy 10-12” P.Z. R025XY014NV site in a former / Artemisia tridentata / Pseudoroegneria spicata - Achnatherum thurberianum 
(/ big sagebrush / bluebunch wheatgrass - Thurber's needlegrass) vegetation community. 
Dry Gulch AIM Plot 01B is located in a Rangeland Shallow Loam 8-12” P.Z. R025XY021NV site in a former / / Artemisia tridentate ssp. wyomingensis / Pseudoroegneria spicata - Achnatherum thurberianum (/ Wyoming big sagebrush / bluebunch wheatgrass - Thurber's needlegrass) vegetation community. 
The Bitterbrush Drill Treatment seed mix was applied via rangeland drill to the public burned land in accordance with the ecological sites and elevation and was comprised of Antelope Bitterbrush (Purshia tridentata), Bluebunch Wheatgrass (Pseudoroegneria spicata), Small Burnet (Sanguisorba minor), Blue Flax (Linum perenne), Sainfoin (Onobrychis viciifolia), and Russian Wildrye (Psathyrostachys juncea). 
The Aerial Mid Elevation Treatment seed mix was applied via fixed wing aircraft to the public burned land in accordance with the ecological sites and elevation and was comprised of Wyoming Big Sagebrush (Artemisia tridentata sbsp wyomingensis), Basin Big Sagebrush (Artemisia tridentata sbsp tridentata), and Western Yarrow (Achillea millefolium var occidentalis).
Density Results 
Rehabilitation objectives are considered successfully met when one native forb per square meter, 0.3 native shrubs per square meter, and three grasses per square meter are established. 
2018: The rehabilitation objectives in the first growing season have not been fully met, though there has been shown progress towards success, especially for the seeded grasses. Seeded grasses nearly reached density objectives as there were 2.63 seeded grasses per square meter in the first growing season. The grasses have not developed deep roots, however and the area needs to be rested until the plants achieve more robust basal and canopy growth. Seeded forbs have achieved an average density of 0.13 per square meter. Seeded antelope bitterbrush shrubs were not found in first year monitoring. The insufficient snowpack and drought-like summer conditions may have contributed to the inability of the shrubs to establish in the area. 
2019: No seeded species were observed. Notably, seeded bitterbrush were also not observed this year. However, native recovery of large-form grasses (squirreltail and Thurber’s needlegrass) and small-form grasses (Sandberg bluegrass and thickspike wheatgrass) was still evident. This is unexpected given the improved weather conditions over the past year. 
2020: Seeded grasses were observed. Bluebunch wheatgrass was the primary observed seeded grass. There were no other seeded species observed through density. 
2022: The rehabilitation objectives for this treatment have been met. Native regrowth of perennial grasses has been very successful at a combined total of 34.8/m2, perennial forbs at 8.8/m2, and shrubs at 1.3/m2. Seeded species have not been as successful as the native regrowth but shrubs and grasses are present and given more time have a chance of continuing progress towards greater rehabilitation of the plots.
AIM Data Results 
Cover 
2018: Foliar cover eclipsed the bare ground in the first growing season, mostly due to the 22% invasive annual desert madwort cover, 23% cheatgrass cover, 20% Sandberg’s bluegrass cover. Perennial forbs have not produced significant cover yet (1.9%). Seeded species haven’t produced significant cover either, as is expected in an area with so much annual, invasive plant competition. 
2019: Perennial grasses dominated foliar cover (39.7%), primarily due to the presence of Sandberg’s bluegrass (28.3%). Second and third highest cover were cheatgrass (24.0%) and desert madwort (18.0%). The dominant cover change is an improvement from 2018. Seeded species did not contribute to cover. 
2020: Perennial grasses continued to dominate foliar cover, primarily due to the presence of Sandberg bluegrass, bluebunch wheatgrass, and thickspike wheatgrass. Cheatgrass levels are still approximately the same while desert madwort cover has reduced since 2019 observations. Perennial species collectively have more cover than annual species. 
2022: Total foliar cover was moderately high at 72.3% with perennial grasses dominating at 31.3%, followed by annual forbs (11.1%) and annual grasses (10.2%). Annual forbs were the only indicator that had an increase in foliar cover from 2020 and it was very minimal. All other indicators had a decrease in cover, the most substantial being annual grasses, down by 10.8% since 2020. Overall, perennial species still constitute more of the cover than annuals though they have gotten closer to being equal since 2020.
Gaps and Erosion 
2018: Gaps in canopy cover were significant and the largest number were greater than 200 centimeters long, the largest measured threshold category. Canopy gaps of this size and frequency have allowed wind and water erosion to occur on the plots, degrading the hydrologic function and soil and site stability. Over 50% of the surface area consists of gaps greater than 25 centimeters. Wind and water erosion were affecting the soil and site stability on both plots: there was rarely occurring deposition and run-off. Commonly occurring pedestals with rarely exposed roots were also present. 
2019: Canopy gaps were mostly between 25 and 50cm long and represented 26.7% of the average 25m transects. Canopy gaps have decreased on the plots since 2018 observations. Similar rare deposition/runoff observations were made along with reduced pedestalling and increased water flow patterns. Reduced observations of pedestals, deposition/runoff, and water flow patterns were made, indicating more stability on the site. 
2020: Canopy gaps were mostly between 51 and 100 cm long, and only by a small amount greater than the 25 to 50 cm long category. Gaps now represent 22.8% of the average 25m transects, which is a decrease from 2019 observations. No pedestalling was observed, along with rare deposition/runoff and water flow patterns, indicating increased soil stability on the site. 
2022: Canopy gaps were predominately between 51-100cm (17.5%), closely followed by 25-50cm (14.7%), and gaps >200cm were observed again (3.7%) after not being observed in 2020. The majority of the gaps being in the smaller size ranges is better for the overall plot health and the 3.7% >200cm consisted of two gaps meeting that criteria across both plots. No observations of site and soil instability was observed on either plot, indicating improvement of soil and site stability across the plots.
Species Richness
2022: Species richness was moderately high with 28 individual species identified on average between the two plots. Perennial forbs and grasses outnumbered their annual counterparts and with four shrub species in addition to the perennials the diversity of species on the plots indicate the possibility of continued improvement on the site.
Recommendations 
2018: Monitoring results in the treatment area have shown that rehabilitation objectives have not been fully met in the first growing season. Although the area had a successful number of bluebunch wheatgrass seedlings establish, those plants need an additional two growing seasons in order to develop the beneficial and stabilizing root masses. The area needs to remain closed so seeded forb and shrub species may establish, especially the antelope bitterbrush which is at risk in the area of not recovering and providing valuable forage to wildlife. If the area receives sufficient snowpack and spring and summer precipitation, seeded species will continue to establish. 
2019: Monitoring results in the treatment area have shown that rehabilitation objectives have not been fully met in the second growing season. Fewer seeded species observations were made this year. This is unexpected given the improved weather conditions over the past year. There was an allotment closure issued for the Gamble Individual allotment, Granite Creek pasture where Plots 01A and 01B are located. The allotment closure objective of three perennial species per square meter was met but it is advised that the area receives appropriate rest so that seeded forb and shrub species may establish, especially the antelope bitterbrush which is at risk in the area of not recovering and providing valuable forage to wildlife. 
2020: Monitoring results in the treatment area have shown that rehabilitation objectives have not been fully met in the third growing season. More seeded grass observations were made this year. There was an allotment closure issued for the Gamble Individual allotment, Granite Creek pasture where Plots 01A and 01B are located. The allotment closure objective of three perennial species per square meter was met but it is advised that the area receives appropriate grazing management so that seeded forb and shrub species may establish. 
2022: The rehabilitation objectives for these plots have been met. The native regrowth on the plots were significant enough to meet the objectives while the seeded species continued to show improvement towards the rehabilitation of the site. There was an allotment closure issued for the Gamble Individual allotment, Granite Creek pasture where Plots 01A and 01B are located. The allotment closure objective of three perennial species per square meter was met and it is advised that the area continues to receive appropriate grazing management so that seeded forb and shrub species may continue to establish.

2022 ESR Monitoring Results
S3 Aerial Mid-Elevation Seeding
Dry Gulch AIM Plot 02 is located in a Rangeland Loamy 12-14” P.Z. R025XY027NV site in a former / Artemisia tridentata ssp. Tridentata / Festuca idahoensis (/ basin big sagebrush / Idaho fescue) vegetation community.
The Aerial Mid Elevation Treatment seed mix was applied via fixed wing aircraft to the public burned land in accordance with the ecological sites and elevation and was comprised of Wyoming Big Sagebrush (Artemisia tridentata sbsp wyomingensis), Basin Big Sagebrush (Artemisia tridentata sbsp tridentata), and Western Yarrow (Achillea millefolium var occidentalis).
Density Results
Rehabilitation objectives are considered successfully met when one native forb per square meter and 0.3 native shrubs per square meter per square meter are established.
2022: The rehabilitation objectives for this treatment have been met with native forb density being observed at 4.4/m2 and shrub density being observed at 1.3/m2, meeting the criteria. Native regrowth of both large form and small form grasses were observed on the plot as well. Seeded species, however, have not been as successful with only 0.3 shrubs/m2 observed on the plot.
AIM Data Results
Cover
2022: Total foliar cover was moderately high at 78.7%, dominated by annual grasses (25.5%), perennial grasses (17.9%), and annual forbs (15.11%). Shrubs were also present (2.4%) but no perennial forbs were observed, same as was observed in 2020.
Gaps and Erosion
2022: Gaps on the plot increased significantly from 2020’s observations with only 25-50cm range having a reduction, though it was only by 1.0%. One gully and few waterflow patterns were observed on plot. When combined with the increase of gaps these observations could be the beginning signals of increased soil instability and plot degradation.
Species Richness
2022: Species richness was high for this plot, increasing by 10 species since the 2019 monitoring season. The number of annual forbs increased by 5 species but perennial species increased by 5 species as well, maintaining that perennial species outnumber the annual species.

S3 Aerial West Mix Seeding
Density Results
Rehabilitation objectives are considered successfully met when one forb per square meter, 0.3 native shrubs per square meter, and three grasses per square meter are established.
2018: The rehabilitation objectives in the first growing season have not been met, though there is evidence of progress towards success. There were 0.17 seeded forbs per square meter in first year monitoring. Neither seeded shrub nor seeded grass seedlings were found in the treatment area. The lack of winter precipitation in the 2017-2018 winter and the drought-like summer conditions may have contributed to the inability of the sagebrush and grasses to establish and persist on the sites.
2019: No seeded shrubs were observed but some seeded forbs and grasses were observed and included Lewis’s flax, Western yarrow, and Sandberg’s bluegrass (which could have been native recovery). Some large-form native grass regrowth (Thurber’s needlegrass and Squirreltail) was observed but no small-form grasses were observed. It was expected that more seeded species establishment and native recovery would be observed given the improved weather conditions over the past year.
2020: No seeded shrubs or forbs were observed. Seeded grasses were observed in abundance in density measurements. Recovery of Thurber’s needlegrass was also evident.
2022: Rehabilitations objectives were met when combining seeded and native forb density on the plot along with 0.3/m2 shrubs observed and the 16.8/m2 seeded grasses observed. Large and small form perennial grasses were the most abundant in the density plots and when combined with the forbs and shrubs observed indicate continued improvement and rehabilitation on the plot.
AIM Data Results
Cover
2018: Average foliar canopy cover was 66.7% in the treatment area in 2018 and bare ground was low due to the prevalence of cheatgrass foliar cover (51.3%) and litter (52%). Perennial grasses were competing with 13.3%, with supporting perennial forbs only producing 1.4% cover. Seeded species were not greatly contributing to cover, most likely due to the cheatgrass competition and somewhat the established perennial grass competition.
2019: Foliar cover increased overall on the plot. Annual grasses (cheatgrass) still are the dominant functional group (69.3%) on the site, followed by perennial grasses (34.0%). All functional groups increased except for shrubs. Bluebunch wheatgrass and Sandbergs bluegrass had the second and third highest cover on the site (18.0% and 14.0% respectively).
2020: Foliar cover was dominated by cheatgrass, followed by bluebunch wheatgrass, Sandberg bluegrass, and desert madwort. Because of cheatgrass cover, annual species collectively have higher cover than perennial species.
2022: Total foliar cover was moderately high at 78.7%, dominated by annual grass (cheatgrass) at 26.3%, followed by 20.3% perennial grasses. Although the annual grass constitutes more cover than the perennial grasses, it would still appear that rehabilitation progress is being made since annual grasses did decrease by half since 2020.
Gaps and Erosion
2018: Gaps in canopy cover that were the size and frequency observed in this aerial seeding treatment have not allowed significant wind and water erosion to occur on the plots. The hydrologic function and soil/site stability were not impaired by the gaps in canopy cover.
Species richness: Twenty-eight different plant species were observed within the 2,827.4 square meter monitoring plot. Wind and water erosion were minimally affecting the soil and site stability on the plot: there were only moderately long and rare water flow patterns, rare deposition/run-off, and common pedestals.
2019: Canopy gaps were primarily greater than 200cm and represented 70% of the average 25m transects. Canopy cover was reduced notably from the first monitoring year. Increased large gaps are a concern for soil site stability. Similar observations of rare deposition/runoff were made on the plot, along with reduced observations or pedestals and water flow patterns. This indicates increased site stability, despite the presence of increased canopy gaps.
2020: Canopy gaps were primarily between 25 and 50 cm long and represented 8.9% of the average 25m transects. These gaps are greatly reduced from 2019 observations, indicating more stability on the site. The same rare pedestalling and water flow patterns were observed, and no deposition/runoff was observed. This indicates improvement in site stability.
2022: Canopy gaps increased greatly from the 2020 monitoring season across every size range. The decrease in cheatgrass is likely contributing to the increased gap, especially since the only sign of erosion on the plot are water flow patterns, indicating maintained site stability.
Species Richness
2022: Species richness was moderately high on this plot with perennial species outnumbering their annual counterparts. Annual forbs increased by 2 species but perennial grasses increased by 3, maintaining the dominance of perennial species.
Recommendations:
2018: Monitoring results in the treatment area have shown that rehabilitation objectives have not been met in the first growing season, although the area has adequate regrowth from established, native perennial grasses. Lower snowpack and drought like conditions in the first growing season have hindered the treatment’s success. The area needs to remain closed for another growing season so seeded species may establish, especially the sagebrush, which was lost from the site.
2019: Monitoring results in the treatment area have shown that rehabilitation objectives have been partially met in the second growing season, although the area has adequate regrowth from established, native perennial grasses. There was an allotment closure issued for the Little Goose Creek allotment, Mustang Draw pasture where Plot 20 is located. The allotment closure objective of three perennial species per square meter was met but it is advised that the area is given additional rest so seeded species may establish, especially the sagebrush, which was lost from the site.
2020: Monitoring results in the treatment area have shown that rehabilitation objectives have been partially met in the third growing season, although the area has adequate regrowth from established, native perennial grasses. There was an allotment closure issued for the Little Goose Creek allotment, Mustang Draw pasture where Plot 20 is located. The allotment closure objective of three perennial species per square meter was met but it is advised that the area is given proper grazing management so seeded species may establish, especially the sagebrush, which was lost from the site.
2022: Monitoring results in the treatment area have shown that rehabilitation objectives have been met and that native regrowth on the plot indicates that continued improvement on the site is possible. There was an allotment closure issued for the Little Goose Creek allotment, Mustang 
Draw pasture where Plot 20 is located. The allotment closure objective of three perennial species per square meter was met but it is advised that the area continues to receive proper grazing management so seeded species may establish.

S3 Aerial Mid-Elevation, Imazapic
Density Results
Rehabilitation objectives are considered successfully met when one native forb per square meter and 0.3 native shrubs per square meter per square meter are established.
2022: Rehabilitation objectives have not been met for this treatment though this is the closest to achieving the goals since monitoring began in 2018. Native regrowth is relatively low as well which could indicate that vegetation seeded and unseeded is struggling to rehabilitate.
AIM Data Results
Cover
2022: Total foliar cover was moderately low at 34.0%, dominated by perennial grasses at 19.1%. The next highest coverage came from annual grasses at 3.6% then perennial forbs at 1.3%, none of the other indicators were observed during the Line-Point Intercept data collection method. While it is not ideal to have such low coverage overall, the large decrease of annual grass cover and maintenance of perennial grass cover is a good sign for the health of the plot.
Gaps and Erosion
2018: Wind and water erosion were minimally affecting the soil and site stability on the plot: there were only short and rare water flow patterns and few pedestals.
2019: Similar (rare) observations of deposition/runoff were made along with increased (common) pedestalling and water flow patterns. This suggests more water erosion on the site and slight changes in soil stability.
2020: Similar common pedestalling and rare deposition/runoff but no water flow patterns were observed on the site, indicating increased site stability.
2022: Canopy gap cover increased significantly from 2020 to 2022, the most concerning being the increase of gaps >200cm from 0.0% to 48.8%, along with the increase of gaps 101-200cm from 0.7% to 21.1%. This large increase in gaps in conjunction with the decreased foliar cover and common waterflow patterns observed on the plot are indicators of soil erosion and plot degradation.
Species Richness
2022: Species richness was moderate on the plot with 23 individual species identified. Perennial species increased by 6 species while annual species decreased by one, meaning that perennial species continue to outnumber the annuals.
Recommendations
2022: Monitoring results in the treatment area have shown that rehabilitation objectives have not been met and that native regrowth of the area does not compensate for the lack of seeded species success. There was an allotment closure issued for the Little Goose Creek, Bluff Creek, and Gamble Individual allotments. The allotment closure objective of three perennial species per square meter was not met and it is advised that the area is given proper grazing management so seeded forbs and sagebrush species may establish.

Objectives: Establish perennial grasses and forbs within 3 years using a native dominated seed mix.
Planned_Implementation: Drill seeding 40,000 acres
Actual_Implementation:
Approximately 34,706 acres were drill seeded starting in the fall of 2010 and completed in spring of 2011. ESR specialists monitored conditions and activities during treatment implementation.
This treatment consisted of five projects; Long Butte North, Long Butte Bombing Range, Long Butte Wild Horse Management Area, Long Butte South, and Long Butte Fuel Breaks (see attached map). Long Butte North consisted of 6,200 acres spread across approximately twelve separate blocks of land. The largest block was several thousand acres and the smallest plots were wildlife tracts of forty acres. The project started on November 1, 2010 with contractor Richard Barney and stopped on November 26th due to environmental conditions. The contractor continued seeding in the spring once conditions improved and was completed on February 21, 2011. The seed mix for this project was identified in the plan as the North Mix and consisted of Great Basin wildrye, bluebunch wheatgrass, Indian ricegrass, bottlebrush squirreltail, Siberian wheatgrass, globemallow, blue flax, and alfalfa.
Long Butte Bombing Range consisted of 3,180 acres in a single block of land. The project started on October 30, 2010 and was completed on November 4, 2010. Boise District BLM operations and fire staff provided personnel and equipment for the project. The seed mix for this project was North Mix.
Long Butte Wild Horse Management Area consisted of 20,326 acres in a single block of land. The project started on November 5, 2010 with Boise and Twin Falls District ESR, operations, and fire personnel. The project was stopped on November 29th due to environmental conditions. Personnel resumed seeding in the spring and completed the project on March 15, 2011. The seed mix for this project was North Mix.
Treatment_Effect_and_Results: Within the Long Butte North project area cheatgrass and sandberg bluegrass were the dominant vegetation throughout the seeded areas. Snake River wheatgrass, Great Basin wildrye, alfalfa, and Wyoming big sagebrush were detected in the southern block of the project area. Fire ecologists site visit during the summer noted the primary vegetation cover consisted of cheatgrass, sandberg bluegrass, and tumble mustard. Cheatgrass growth was extensive in some areas.\r\nCheatgrass and sandberg bluegrass dominated the cover in the Bombing Range project area but Snake River wheatgrass and bottlebrush squirreltail were detected in the both the cover transects and density frames. Alfalfa and sagebrush was also detected in the density frames.\r\nThe Wild Horse Management area is dominated by cheatgrass, crested wheatgrass, and sandberg bluegrass. Some alfalfa, Wyoming big sagebrush, bluebunch wheatgrass, bottlebrush squirreltail, and Great Basin wildrye were detected either in the cover transect or the density frames. A site visit by the fire ecologists during the summer noted the area appeared to primarily cheatgrass, sandberg bluegrass, with crested wheat seedings and some tumble mustard. In some parts of the area cheatgrass was thick and tall, up to three feet in height.

PART 9 – RECOMMENDATIONS/CONCLUSIONS 
The Black Point fire will continue to have residual effects across the landscape for many years, but the planning, treatments, and monitoring accomplished in the last year have provided a steppingstone to continue with the restoration efforts throughout the burn area. One of the biggest lessons learned is that restoration takes time when you are dealing with environmental effects. There are many factors that go into restoring burn areas, some are human, but many are environmental. Goals and objectives will continue to be developed for restoring the Black Point Fire and the lessons learned from this fire will be used for future planning in Emergency Stabilization and Rehabilitation.

Treatment/Activity: S2 Ground Seeding The RMP states under the Soil, Water, and Air
Section (II-: 78) that BLM should, "minimize soil erosion by maintaining good, perennial
vegetation cover on all sites." The RMP also states under the range improvement section (p II-
80 & 81) that, "interseeding and reseeding projects in MUAs1 with objectives to maintain
wildlife habitat ... will use shrub, forb, and grass seed mixtures that are normally found in that
type of ecological zone/type." The RMP in the Rehabilitation Section (p. II-89) states "Seeding
will include appropriate seed mixtures to replace wildlife habitat that is burned." The proposed
seeding will help stabilize soils, reduce the potential for introduction and spread of non-native
invasive plants and noxious weeds, and improve wildlife habitat.

burned area (944 acres) with a mixture of Anatone Bluebunch and Vavilov Siberian wheatgrass,
Appar Blue Flax and Ladak Alfalfa. Seeding would occur shortly after approval of the plan and

Treatment_Effect_and_Results:
Examination of the burned area on a June 6, 2013, site visit by the fire ecologist revealed that seeding establishment was spotty. Some areas had large patches of well-established seeded species. Other areas were dominated by cheatgrass and/or on-site natives including Sandberg bluegrass and bottlebrush squirreltail. Seeded species were observed to be present in drill rows in these areas, but at much lower density.

Monitoring results for 2014 indicate good recovery of on-site native perennial grasses and crested wheatgrass, with some establishment of seeded species. Cheatgrass is steadily decreasing in both cover and density.

CLOSEOUT CONCLUSIONS: The area was dominated by Wyoming big sagebrush prior to burning. The crested wheatgrass in the understory was undetected – this often occurs in areas with old seedings that have been reinvaded by sagebrush. The crested wheatgrass is resilient following fire, but may compete to some degree with seeded species. This competition with seeded species has been observed with other recent ESR projects. However, seeding following fire can help diversify old seedings where the plants are not dense and can fill in areas not previously seeded.
Between seeding and natural recovery of perennial plants, the burned area is stable against dominance by invasive species and erosion by water and wind. One of the greatest threats to the site appears to be continued encroachment of Scotch thistle from adjacent private land.

Two years post-treatment the total density of seeded grass species on the Geothermal ESR project was 5.8 plants/m2, exceeding the treatment objective (Table 3). Siberian wheatgrass (Agropyron fragile) and Russian wildrye varieties (Psathyrostachys juncea) dominated, with Snake River wheatgrass (Elymus wawawaiensis) also present (Tables 3-4). Treatment_Effect_and_Results:
ESR 2022 Monitoring Report
R2 Ground, R3 Aerial Seeding
Goose AIM Plot 04 was correlated to a Ceanothus Thicket site on a former Ceanothus velutinus (snowbrush ceanothus) vegetation site on a hill backslope.
Drill seed mix consisted of Snake River wheatgrass (Elymus wawawaiensis), Sherman bluegrass (Poa secunda), Indian ricegrass (Achnatherum hymenoides), and Dryland alfalfa (Medicago sp.).
Density Results:
2020: The drill and aerial overseeding of this portion of the fire has not been completed. The pre-treatment of the area with aerial imazapic (herbicide) was completed by the Nevada Department of Wildlife. A range of 1 to 7 different perennial species was observed within AIM Plot 04’s density frames.
2021: The rehab objective of 3 seeded bunchgrasses, 1 native forb, and 0.3 shrubs per square meter has not been fully met. No seeded species were observed in the density frames, however native regrowth of forbs and shrubs met the objective goals. Where there were plants observed in 2020 the numbers have decreased in 2021.
2022: The rehabilitation objectives have not been met, again due to a lack of seeded grasses and seeded forbs present. Seeded and native regrowth of perennial grasses was relatively high at 10.5/m2 collectively. Native regrowth of forbs and shrubs are also showing signs of establishment on the plot.
AIM Data Results:
Cover
2020: Average foliar canopy cover was over all very low (11.3%) with a large amount of bare ground (50.7%). Plant cover observations through LPI were primarily perennial species with the exception of the presence of yellow salsify. No cheatgrass observations were made in LPI measurements.
2021: Average foliar canopy cover decreased from the low 11.3% last year to 10.67% in 2021. No annuals were observed during Line-Point Intercept though they were observed on the plot. Shrubs increased by 2% but perennial forbs decreased 2.7% from 4.7% in 2020. While annuals have not established dominance on the site there is potential for that since there aren’t many perennials established either.
2022: Average foliar canopy cover increased since 2021 by 6% but still remains low at 16.7% total. Perennial grasses and shrub dominate the foliar cover at 5.9% and 4.3% respectively. No annual grasses were observed and annual forbs remained very low at only 0.5% observed on plot.
Gaps and Erosion
2020: The percentages of gap ranges were split in two. The two smallest gap ranges (25-50cm and 51-100cm) each had approximately 13% while the two highest gap ranges (101-200cm and >200cm) each had approximately 24%.
No rills, gullies, or sheet erosion were observed on the plot. Widespread pedestalling (commonly exposed roots), common deposition/runoff, and moderately long water flow patterns were observed on the plot. This indicates wind and water erosion are common on the plot which could impact future treatment success.
2021: The most frequently observed gap range was >200cm at 45.7% almost twice what it was in 2020. Additionally, the 101-200 range increased by roughly 6% and the two smallest ranges saw decreases in their frequency. No data was collected about signs of erosion on the plot.
2022: The most frequently observed gap range was still >200cm at 40.0%, a reduction of 5.7% but still a significant amount of coverage. Overall, the distribution of gap across the size ranges remained similar to that observed in 2021. Small amount of pedestaling and deposition were observed across the plot.

Species Richness
2020: Perennials outnumbered annuals and the presence of shrub species is a good sign of soil stability and rehabilitation.
2021: Distribution of species types remained similar to 2020. The biggest change was the loss of 6 perennial forbs and 5 total species observed on plot.
2022: Species richness decreased by only 2 since 2021 but there was a shift in distribution in that perennial grasses lost 4 species and annual forbs gained 3. If this trend continues it could have negative consequences for the future health of the plot.
Recommendations
2021: The ESR rehabilitation objectives of the aerial seedings have not been fully met, although some seeded species have been observed and recovery of perennial species is apparent. There was a grazing closure issued for the Goose fire area. The objective of three perennial grasses per square meter has been met (primarily through Poa species regrowth) in the aerial seeding and imazapic treatment areas. It is advised that the area is reviewed and the fire area receive appropriate rest and grazing management so that seeded species may establish as treatments continue.
2022: The ESR rehabilitation objectives of the aerial seedings have not been fully met, although some seeded species have been observed and recovery of perennial species is apparent. There was a grazing closure issued for the Goose fire area. The objective of three perennial grasses per square meter has been met (primarily through Poa species regrowth) in the aerial seeding and imazapic treatment areas. It is advised that the area is reviewed and the fire area receive appropriate rest and grazing management so that seeded species may establish as treatments continue.
